anti_overlap: Leaves furniture and media economic incentives, pricing curves, and monetization-ethics questions to the economy reviewer.
Leaves walk-loop occupancy resolution order, determinism of who-comes/who-stays, and snapshot-timing semantics to the colony-sim/agent-occupancy reviewer.
Does not challenge the choice of pixel art itself (settled by decision 4 against comp D); reviews only whether the stated production and rendering constraints can actually deliver it as specified.
decision_lens: Authored by code, on a fixed palette, at a scale small enough to remove the face — does the resulting sprite still read as a distinct person against a screen of other identical-format figures, and does the one-screen cross-section actually fit the room count this design promises without becoming either a scroll wearing a camera's name or an unreadable smear?
focus: Whether the pixel-art production pipeline and the fixed one-screen, no-scroll, portrait-first cross-section rendering are technically and visually achievable under the constraints this brainstorm sets — no artist, no image model, sprites authored in code, a fixed palette, faceless figures, and framed photographs composited into drawn pixel rooms.
name: fd-pixelart-fixedcamera
persona: Apply the perspective of a pixel-art technical director and mobile 2D rendering engineer who has shipped code-authored sprite pipelines for small teams without dedicated artists, specializing in fixed-palette tile and sprite systems, small-scale character legibility, and camera-versus-scroll layout design on portrait phone viewports.
review_areas: Decision 5 (met = drawn, no face; unmet = silhouette; identity carried by hair, shirt, build, hat) at pixel-art figure scale within a stacked, one-screen cross-section: verify the implied sprite grid leaves enough pixels for those four identity slots to actually distinguish a dozen-plus met regulars from each other at a glance, rather than collapsing into visual noise once more than a few regulars share a screen.

Decision 4 (pixel art on a fixed palette; per-room wall/trim/floor palettes as comp C drew them) against decision 9 (photographs hang framed IN the drawn room, and conjure retires so 'the frame is the whole of it'): specify how a raster, photographic framed picture composites against a fixed, limited pixel palette without either the photo reading as a jarring foreign object or the palette being widened to accommodate arbitrary photo colors, which would break 'fixed palette.'

OQ1 (how many rooms fit one phone screen before the stack needs a panning camera) against decision 1 (one screen, no document scroll, now written as law) and decision 3 (portrait phone first, desktop 'same stack, wider'): once room count exceeds what a portrait screen draws at legible sprite scale, a panning camera under a player's thumb is functionally close to the scrolling this whole brainstorm exists to refuse — verify the document draws the camera/scroll line precisely enough that an implementer can't rebuild the rejected interaction under a new name.

OQ5 (sprite order: which of the 36 authored symbols get sprites first, with the art gate being 'mk sees their own rooms moving before the economy lands'): verify the pipeline for turning 36 existing authored symbols into consistent-quality, code-authored pixel sprites is specified enough to avoid the 'uneven first-pass sprites' risk the document itself names, given zero art staff and no image-model tooling in-house.

The walk/idle/speak figure loop against a no-artist production constraint: 'walk between rooms, idle, and speak moment lines' implies multiple animation states per figure per identity-slot combination (hair × shirt × build × hat); verify the design acknowledges the combinatorial sprite/animation surface this creates and names how a from-scratch pipeline keeps it from becoming its own unbounded production burden.

Per-room visual budget: a fixed camera showing multiple simultaneously visible rooms, each potentially holding a framed founding photo, a 'what's on' media slot, and one or more furniture pieces, all inside one small drawn cell — verify a defined visual hierarchy or slot budget exists so these elements don't compete for the same scarce pixel real estate the one-screen constraint already makes tight.
severity_examples: P0: the room-stack must fit an arbitrary player's full room count on one portrait screen with no scroll (decision 1, a hard law), and no upper bound on room count is set anywhere else in the document; a player with enough rooms shrinks every sprite — including the hair/shirt/build/hat identity detail decision 5 depends on — below pixel-legible size, silently breaking the signature figures mechanic with no plan-level room-count decision (OQ1 explicitly defers it) positioned to catch this before it's built.

P1: the 'camera that pans' OQ1 names as the only escape once rooms exceed one screen is implemented as a thumb-draggable or auto-scrolling viewport over a house taller than the display, reproducing the exact scrolling interaction mk called 'an absolute dealbreaker' for the prior journal-home surface under a different name — and nothing in decisions 1-13 draws the camera/scroll line precisely enough to prevent it.

P2: turning the 36 existing authored symbols (decision 9, 'become catalog stock') into pixel sprites has no specified per-symbol production checklist (silhouette shape, palette assignment, size class), so sprite quality visibly varies piece to piece the first time mk sees the room populated — exactly the 'uneven first-pass' risk OQ5 already names as caught only by mk's own late-stage art-gate review, an expensive point to catch a problem a lightweight spec could catch earlier.
success_hints: Grounds findings in the specific decisions and open questions from the document (1, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, OQ1, OQ5) rather than generic pixel-art advice.

Treats 'no document scroll, ever' (decision 1, elevated to law) as the single hardest constraint in the document, and checks every camera/pan/layout proposal against literally reproducing scroll under another name.

Distinguishes an achievable-but-unspecified production detail (fine to leave to plan-level) from a physically or visually impossible combination of constraints — e.g. unbounded room count plus a fixed screen plus legible small-scale identity encoding — that no plan can resolve without a design-level decision this document should make now.
Names the concrete on-screen failure (an illegible sprite, scroll-in-disguise, a clashing palette) for each finding rather than an abstract art-production complaint.
Stays inside sprite/pixel production, palette, camera/layout, and screen-space budget territory; leaves currency/pricing and agent-occupancy/simulation-determinism questions to the other reviewers.
task_context: Target: the cross-section brainstorm at docs/brainstorms/2026-09-02-cross-section-brainstorm.md, in which the home surface becomes a drawn pixel-art cross-section of the player's rooms on one screen, Uncs walk between rooms, media draws who comes, furniture shapes who stays, furniture is bought with steps, and the journal is demoted to a snapshot record drawer. Apply the pixel-art/mobile-rendering perspective above and stress-test this design: what makes it fail, what is it missing — specifically in the sprite production and fixed-camera rendering dimension: does the identity-encoding figure design survive at the pixel scale a one-screen, multi-room layout forces, does the fixed palette survive compositing raster founding photographs into drawn rooms, does the camera-versus-scroll line hold once room count exceeds one screen, and does the no-artist, code-authored sprite pipeline have a specified path to consistent quality across the 36 symbols awaiting sprites.
